Volume 07 · Chapter 05

Debt, leases and financing obligations

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c04

By the endAnalyze financing obligations and their effects on performance and cash flow.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can reconstruct a borrower's obligations from a dated contract; reconcile cash interest, effective interest and principal; build a lessee's liability and right-of-use schedules; and distinguish a covenant test from a payment forecast. Read asset cost, depreciation and carrying amounts, retain the three-statement cash reconciliation, and use the present-value tools from the time value of money. The accounting equation still governs every entry.

“Debt is 100” is incomplete information. It could mean face amount, net proceeds received, amortized carrying amount, a current market quote or a payment due next week. A lease can create both a useful asset and a payment obligation without a cash purchase at commencement. Begin with the entity, dates and enforceable promises before interpreting a reported total.

1. Identify the obligation and its clock

The borrower receives funding and promises specified payments; the lender holds the corresponding claim. Principal is the contractual amount borrowed or scheduled for repayment under the agreement. A note's face amount is its stated redemption amount. A coupon is a specified cash interest payment, often a percentage of face. A maturity is the date an obligation falls due. An amortizing loan repays principal over time; a bullet note concentrates principal repayment at maturity.

Signing documents, receiving cash, accruing interest and making a payment can occur on different dates. A simple cash loan received at par gives Dr Cash / Cr Loan liability. It is financing, not sales revenue. Interest incurred but unpaid gives Dr Interest expense / Cr Interest payable, or an identified accrual within the debt account. Paying principal reduces cash and liability rather than creating another expense. The labels on an instrument do not settle its classification: a security called a “share” may contain mandatory payment terms that need separate analysis. Our ordinary contributed capital is stipulated residual equity; complex redeemable and compound instruments are outside this chapter.

An undrawn facility is not cash already received. A future purchase or lease commitment is not automatically a presently recognized borrowing. Its fees, cancellation terms, commencement and any separately recognizable obligations still need examination. Conversely, an obligation need not disappear from analysis merely because it is absent from one balance-sheet line. Commitments and contingent exposures belong in a dated funding assessment under their actual terms.

Use one period length throughout an interest schedule. A quoted annual nominal rate compounded monthly is not itself a monthly effective rate, and a simple actual-day loan convention is not an annual compound model. Below, one period is a complete year, payments occur after that year's interest accrual, and rates are effective per year. All companies and amounts are original synthetic examples in kCU, thousands of currency units. Calendar labels are supplied assumptions, not observations about a real borrower.

2. Derive amortized carrying value from promised cash

For the bounded fixed-payment model, let P₀ > 0 be initial net carrying value, r ≥ 0 the supplied effective annual rate, and Mₜ ≥ 0 the total cash payment at each year-end t = 1,…,n. M includes that date's coupon and any principal. Assume at least one positive payment, fixed terms, no default, modification, foreign currency, embedded option or fair-value remeasurement. The instrument's eligibility for the stated amortized-cost convention is supplied.

P₀ = Σt=1n Mₜ/(1+r)ᵗ.
Interest expense Jₜ = rPₜ₋₁.
Closing carrying value Pₜ = Pₜ₋₁ + Jₜ − Mₜ.

Multiply the initial present value by 1+r and subtract M₁: what remains is the present value, at date 1, of payments still due. Repeating the same step proves by induction

Pₜ = Σs=t+1n Mₛ/(1+r)s−t, so Pₙ = 0.
Σ Jₜ = Σ Mₜ − P₀.

The final equality also follows by summing the carrying-value rollforward and canceling intermediate balances. It is an independent lifetime check: expense allocates the difference between all repayments and initial net funding. A final unexplained “plug” to zero conceals a wrong rate, payment, fee or rounding convention. When r = 0, value equals the undiscounted remaining payments and effective interest is zero.

If the rate is unknown, the present-value function is continuous and strictly decreasing for r ≥ 0: each positive dated payment has derivative −tMₜ/(1+r)t+1 < 0. It equals ΣMₜ at zero and tends to zero as r grows. Thus 0 < P₀ < ΣMₜ gives exactly one positive rate; equality gives zero. Net proceeds greater than all payments do not fit a nonnegative-rate model. This uniqueness argument relies on a conventional initial funding receipt followed by nonnegative payments; it does not prove uniqueness for arbitrary cash streams with changing signs. Our examples supply a rate and verify it rather than requiring a numerical solver.

For equal coupons C and final face F, with no fees, let A(r) = Σ(1+r)−t. The geometric-series identity F = rF A(r) + F/(1+r)ⁿ gives P₀−F = (C−rF)A(r). Since A(r) is positive, coupon rate C/F above r produces a premium, issue value above face; below r produces a discount. At r = 0 the same identity reads P₀−F = nC. A zero-coupon note can still have interest expense: its initial value grows toward the larger redemption payment.

MIT's 2003 debt notes distinguish coupon, issue-date effective rate and later market yield. A later change in market yield can change the price of the lender's claim without changing this fixed amortized-cost schedule. Carrying value is not automatically the amount required for early settlement or the amount a lender could obtain by selling the claim.

Fees change net funding, not the promised face amount

Under our stipulated eligible-cost convention, directly attributable issue costs reduce the borrower's initial liability carrying amount and are included in its effective interest. Let gross lender proceeds be V and the eligible cash fee f: P₀ = V−f. Record gross funding and the fee separately, even when their net amount is the number used in the yield equation. A fee for a separate service is not automatically such a financing cost.

The inspected December 2022 Australian AASB 9 compilation provides scoped support for transaction-cost-adjusted measurement and the effective-interest definition, including integral fees and premiums/discounts. Its version applies to specified historical reporting periods; we use the method explicitly, without claiming a complete current standard comparison. Do not import the lender's asset-classification tests into every borrower liability, or lower promised repayments merely because the borrower hopes not to pay them.

Worked example 1 — Three initial amounts and two kinds of interest

Ridgeway Tool Hire receives lender cash of 102 on 1 January 2025 and immediately pays an eligible issue fee of 2. It promises a coupon of 8 on 31 December 2025 and a coupon of 8 plus face 104.2 on 31 December 2026. The effective annual rate on net funding is 10%. There are no other fees, unpaid coupons or changes to the contract.

Net P₀ = 102−2 = 100.
8/1.10 + 112.2/1.10² = 100.

Face is 104.2; gross proceeds are 102; net proceeds and initial carrying value are 100. The gross issue discount is 2.2, while face less net carrying value is 4.2, including the eligible fee. The annual cash coupon rate is 8/104.2 ≈ 7.678%, which is neither the effective 10% nor a later market yield.

Ridgeway note schedule, kCU; payments after annual accrual
DateOpening carrying valueEffective interestCoupon cashFace repaidClosing carrying value
31 Dec 20251001080102
31 Dec 202610210.28104.20

At commencement, record Dr Cash 102 / Cr Note liability 102, then Dr Note liability 2 / Cr Cash 2. Net liability is 100; alternatively, a gross-face ledger could show an unamortized discount/cost contra account. Do not deduct that contra amount twice. We use one net note account.

In year 1, Dr Interest expense 10 / Cr Note liability 10, then Dr Note liability 8 / Cr Cash 8. Net accretion is 2. In year 2, accrue 10.2 and settle the resulting liability of 112.2 with cash. Effective interest totals 20.2, equal to total payments 120.2 less initial net proceeds 100. Coupons total only 16; the remaining 4.2 of expense allocates the discount and fee. There is no additional expense merely because the final face amount is large.

3. A lease liability and a right-of-use asset have different jobs

A lessee obtains a right to use an asset; the lessor supplies that right. Recognition is not established merely by calling a service contract a lease. For our model, control of the use of an identified asset throughout the stated term is stipulated, the asset is available at commencement, and no recognition exemption is taken. We study the lessee's records only.

Let L₀ be the present value of lease payments still unpaid at commencement, discounted at a supplied appropriate periodic rate i. A right-of-use asset, R, records the recognized resource; the lease liability records the payment obligation. With no initial prepayment, incentive, direct lease cost or restoration obligation, R₀ = L₀. If a separately stated commencement payment A₀ is already paid, our simplified initial asset is R₀ = L₀ + A₀; the same A₀ must not remain in the unpaid-liability PV.

L₀ = Σ Mlease,t/(1+i)ᵗ.
Lₜ = Lₜ₋₁ + iLₜ₋₁ − Mlease,t.
With a zero-residual right expiring after n years: annual ROU depreciation = R₀/n.

The liability applies effective interest; the asset follows its supplied consumption/depreciation convention from the preceding chapter. The difference is not an accounting error. Payment principal is cash payment less that period's interest in our positive-amortization examples. Total lease expense combines depreciation and interest; it need not equal cash rent each year. Initial noncash recognition is disclosed as such rather than creating fictional cash received and paid.

The IFRS Foundation's September 2020 investor explanation describes this distinction between the right-of-use asset, a present-value obligation, depreciation and interest. Actual term and discount-rate selection, exemptions, variable rents, renewal or purchase options, incentives, index changes, restoration, impairment and modifications need further facts. Straight-line depreciation over the lease term here depends on no ownership transfer or exercised purchase option and the supplied consumption pattern.

Worked example 2 — A lease asset falls to sixty while its liability is sixty-six

On 1 January 2025 Ridgeway also obtains a two-year equipment-use right. It pays 66 after the first year's accrual and 72.6 after the second, both on 31 December. The supplied rate is 10%. No payment is due at commencement; there is no incentive, initial lease cost, residual guarantee, restoration obligation, extension or ownership transfer. The right expires at the end of 2026 and is consumed evenly.

L₀ = 66/1.10 + 72.6/1.10² = 60 + 60 = 120.
R₀ = 120; annual depreciation = 60.

YearOpening liabilityInterestCash paymentLiability reductionClosing liabilityClosing ROU carrying amountTotal lease expense
2025120126654666072
2026666.672.6660066.6

Initially Dr ROU asset 120 / Cr Lease liability 120. For 2025, Dr Interest expense 12 / Cr Lease liability 12; Dr Lease liability 66 / Cr Cash 66; and Dr Depreciation expense 60 / Cr Accumulated ROU depreciation 60. The expense is 72 while cash paid is 66. At the next close, expense is 66.6 while cash paid is 72.6. Total expense 138.6 equals total payments 138.6 over this complete zero-residual right; their timing differs.

Ridgeway does not own this equipment outright, and a remaining right of use is not assumed freely saleable for its carrying amount. Neither netting the asset against the liability nor omitting both explains the resource and the obligation as clearly as the two schedules.

A bounded comparison with US lease accounting

The FASB's 2016-02 summary, revised June 2020, explains that both finance and operating leases enter the lessee balance sheet under its described model, while their expense and cash-flow presentation differ. Its operating-lease illustration uses a single straight-line lease expense, whereas its finance-lease illustration separates amortization and interest. The summary contrasts that dual model with IFRS 16's lessee approach. Therefore “operating lease” does not by itself mean “no recognized liability.”

We do not determine a US classification for Ridgeway from these few facts, or use the same asset-expense formula for every framework. Our numerical model is the explicitly stipulated separate depreciation/interest convention. A changed presentation can change a reported performance subtotal or CFO without changing contractual payments; compare consistently defined quantities.

4. Put financing, assets, profit and cash into one entity

Complete Ridgeway's model with an ordinary equity contribution of 100 at commencement and an owned equipment purchase of 80. The owned equipment is immediately available, has a four-year life and zero residual, and is depreciated straight-line at 20 per year. It remains in use after the two-year debt/lease horizon. There are no taxes, receivables, inventory, payables, impairment, dividends or other transactions. All operating revenue is collected and all other operating expense paid within the stated year; receipts precede payments in the supplied annual cash ordering. Detailed intra-year funding is not inferred.

The main cash-flow convention puts paid note coupons and paid lease interest in operating cash flow; note face repayments and lease principal reductions in financing; and owned-equipment purchases in investing. At commencement, owner contribution, note proceeds and the eligible issue fee are separately financing. This is a maintained classification for the case, not a blanket claim about every current IFRS 18 or US GAAP presentation. The cash-flow chapter explains why changing interest classification requires a consistent indirect bridge.

Worked example 3 — The full company, including the noncash lease

Commencement cash is 100 + 102 − 2 − 80 = 120. Gross financing receipts are owner 100 plus lender 102; the fee is a financing outflow of 2, giving net financing 200. Investing cash is −80. Recognizing the lease adds asset 120 and liability 120 without cash. Total assets are cash 120 + owned equipment 80 + ROU asset 120 = 320, equal to note 100 + lease liability 120 + equity 100.

Cash revenue is 260 in 2025 and 240 in 2026; other cash operating expense is 140 each year. Operating cash before financing costs is therefore 120 and 100. That subtotal is defined here, not an unexplained “cash earnings” measure.

In 2025, direct CFO = 120−8−12 = 100. Lease principal of 54 is financing; no note face is repaid. Cash rises 100−54 = 46, from 120 to 166. The indirect bridge is profit 18 + depreciation 80 + note discount/fee accretion 2 = 100. Only 8 of the note's expense 10 was cash interest. Do not add all interest back while also leaving paid interest in operating cash.

In 2026, CFO = 100−8−6.6 = 85.4. Financing cash is −104.2−66 = −170.2. Cash falls 84.8 to 81.2. Indirect CFO is 3.2+80+2.2 = 85.4. Repayment of old principal reduces cash and liabilities without reducing profit again. Both modeled liabilities end at zero, while owned equipment and cash remain. That endpoint does not assert that a continuing company will never borrow again.

Those movement calculations start from the separately displayed commencement position. A full-calendar 2025 cash-flow statement starting before formation also includes 1 January: CFO is 100, CFI is −80 and CFF is 200−54 = 146, taking cash from zero to 166. In 2026, CFI is zero and the preceding movement figures already cover the full year. Do not omit the commencement block merely because it was displayed separately for instruction. The benchmark returns both views.

At 31 December 2025 the remaining contractual cash is note 112.2 plus lease 72.6, totaling 184.8, all due within the next year. The carrying liabilities total 168. The 16.8 difference is future effective interest, 10.2 + 6.6, not a missing recognized liability under this model. A maturity table of undiscounted payments and a carrying-value reconciliation serve different purposes.

5. Covenant compliance, liquidity and extinguishment

A covenant is a contractual condition, such as a specified leverage limit, reporting obligation or restriction on asset sales. Its numerator, denominator, adjustments, testing dates and consequences must come from the agreement. Headroom is the distance from that exact limit. A familiar ratio name is not a substitute for the definition, and a lender's discretion or waiver is not automatic.

Ridgeway's fictional agreement tests after the 2025 payments and closing. It requires positive book equity E and D ≤ 1.5E, where D includes the net carrying note and lease liabilities, with no cash netting, and E includes contributed capital plus retained earnings. The base case gives D = 168, E = 118 and headroom 1.5(118)−168 = 9. The ratio is 168/118 = 84/59 ≈ 1.424, so it passes this test.

Now suppose only 2025 cash revenue falls from 260 to 230. Other expense remains 140: operating cash before finance is 90. Profit falls to −12, cash to 136 and equity to 88. Assets 256 still equal liabilities 168 plus equity 88. Headroom is 132−168 = −36: the covenant fails despite cash remaining positive. The program reports the breach; it does not presume acceleration, a waiver, new lending or an accounting gain.

Liquidity asks whether money is available at the required dates. Define a separate descriptive coverage ratio here as operating cash before finance divided by all scheduled note and lease payments. Ridgeway's base ratios are 120/74 = 60/37 in 2025 and 100/184.8 = 125/231 in 2026. The second is below one, yet cash accumulated earlier pays the bills. This coverage measure is not our covenant and does not establish long-run solvency. If equity is zero or negative, a debt/equity quotient is not an informative compliant ratio; our contract explicitly fails that case.

A reporting classification is another question. The IASB's October 2022 announcement explains amendments effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024: covenants to be complied with after the reporting date do not change that date's current/noncurrent classification, but related disclosures convey the risk of early repayment. This scoped statement does not eliminate covenants that already condition settlement rights at the reporting date. Apply the relevant full framework, dates and rights; do not infer a waiver from management's intention to refinance.

Extinguishment means the old obligation is actually discharged, canceled or expires under the applicable terms. In the simple full-settlement case, cash paid above the liability's carrying amount creates a loss; cash paid below it creates a gain. For carrying value P and settlement cash K, record Dr Liability P, Cr Cash K and the balancing gain P−K, or debit loss K−P when negative. The inspected AASB 9 text supports this bounded comparison. It is not permission to remove debt merely because its market price fell, negotiations began or a replacement loan was hoped for. A modification that leaves the old obligation outstanding can require a different analysis.

6. A useful financing note and a reproducible audit

A decision-useful obligation summary connects the recognized balance with the cash and contractual terms. For our case, disclose the borrower and currency, face and net carrying values, coupon and effective rates, eligible issue costs and unamortized amount, dated undiscounted payments, interest/principal classification, and the noncash lease addition. Explain the lease term, discount rate and asset depreciation assumptions. State collateral or guarantees if present; none is supplied here. For a covenant, report its exact scope, testing date, calculated result and actual remedy or unresolved status.

For refinancing and other commitments, distinguish a funded borrowing, a legally available undrawn amount and an unapproved proposal. Record expiry, draw conditions, lender discretion and fees. An undrawn line that expires before the payment date cannot fill that funding gap. A commitment's full face amount is not automatically a recognized debt, but the absence of that amount from the balance sheet does not establish that every fee, guarantee, loss exposure or disclosure requirement is zero. Our numerical model excludes those additional instruments rather than assigning them a universal treatment.

Download the Ridgeway input contract, standard-library benchmark and README together. Run python3 v07-c05-analysis.py. Exact rational kCU calculations preserve the present-value and terminal identities; output such as 406/5 means 81.2 kCU. There is no silent rounding to cash minor units. An actual rounded-payment agreement needs its own explicit last-payment rule.

The benchmark generates journals and closes income accounts, checks every modeled cash prefix, and returns both liability schedules, the ROU/owned carrying amounts, performance, cash bridges and covenant result. Annual receipts are assumed to precede expenses and debt service. Lease payments must cover current interest in this bounded cash-classification model; rent-free or negative-amortization lease periods require a broader allocation rule. A negative cash prefix is rejected as an unfunded proposal. Neither a balanced ledger nor a positive annual cash total proves fine-date liquidity or contractual compliance.

Reproduce the schedules independently before inspecting the code. Then change operating receipts to test the covenant, change a fee without changing the rate to expose an inconsistent contract, and construct a coherent zero-rate case. State what changes in obligations, measurement, profit and cash separately. A later market-price sensitivity should not silently overwrite a fixed effective-interest schedule.

Exercises

Amounts are kCU. Use the chapter's stated recognition, annual timing and cash-classification conventions unless a question changes them. Assume no unlisted transactions, taxes, fees or penalties. Where a contract is changed or settled, that additional agreement is explicitly supplied; do not infer it from a wish to improve a ratio.

  1. Received, accrued and still undrawn. On 1 January a borrower receives a par loan of 60. Its contract uses simple annual interest of 8%; one quarter is exactly one fourth of a year. The first interest payment is due on 1 April, and principal is due two years later. At 31 March, record the initial borrowing and interest accrual, state changes in cash, assets, liabilities and equity, and identify the cash-flow category. A separate facility of 40 remains wholly undrawn with no fee or other recognized obligation in this case. Can the borrower add that 40 to cash or record it as revenue?
  2. A premium reverses the accretion sign. A separate two-year note provides net cash 100 with no issue fee. It pays coupons of 12 each year and final face of 95.8. Verify a 10% effective rate, construct the complete carrying-value schedule, compare expense with coupon cash, and verify lifetime expense. Explain the sign of the premium amortization and why the final face payment is not a new operating expense.
  3. A zero coupon with two positive financing costs. A one-year note promises only 126 at maturity, with no separate coupon. The lender pays 120 at issuance, while an eligible directly attributable issue fee of 7.5 is paid immediately. Find net funding, the one-year effective rate and expense, and compare the effective rate with the no-fee yield on gross proceeds. Give the initial and maturity entries and show why expensing the fee at commencement while also using the fee-adjusted interest expense duplicates its cost.
  4. Prepaid lease cash is not still unpaid. An eligible two-year right is available at date 0. A payment of 55 is made immediately, followed by 60.5 at date 1 and 66.55 at date 2. The effective annual lease rate is 10%; there is no ownership transfer, residual, incentive, other cost or impairment. Calculate initial liability and ROU asset, both annual liability/interest schedules, straight-line ROU depreciation, annual total expense and lifetime cash/expense reconciliation. Explain the error in including the paid 55 again in the liability.
  5. Change classification consistently. Use Ridgeway's complete base case. For comparison only, put all paid note and lease interest in financing instead of operating; keep every recognition, measurement and cash date fixed. Recalculate CFO, CFF and indirect CFO for movements after commencement in each year, and give the combined full-calendar 2025 cash-flow categories. Explain whether either year's total cash, profit or covenant result changes. Do not claim that a larger CFO by itself demonstrates better operations.
  6. Two explicitly permitted covenant repairs. Use the year-1 revenue stress: debt 168, equity 88 and cash 136. The lender now permits either an ordinary cash equity injection just before a repeat test or a partial note retirement at its carrying amount with no gain, loss or fee. It agrees to those treatments for the repeat covenant D ≤ 1.5E. Calculate the minimum amount for each separate remedy and each resulting cash, assets, debt and equity. Compare liquidity. What additional contract information is required before forecasting later note payments after the partial retirement?
  7. A maturity gap and an expiring line. Start Ridgeway's second year from the base first-year balance sheet, including cash 166 and equity 118. Replace second-year cash revenue by 160 while other cash operating expense stays 140; retain all scheduled depreciation and debt/lease payments. Management requires cash of at least 10 after settlement. A wholly undrawn line of 50 expires before the payment date and cannot be drawn or renewed; a proposed replacement has no commitment. Find closing cash without new funding, profit and the financing required to preserve the buffer. If a new loan for exactly that amount is actually funded immediately before settlement, with no fee and interest beginning only after the close, reconcile closing assets, liabilities and equity. Has total debt disappeared?
  8. Market price, book amount and actual retirement. At Ridgeway's base year-1 reporting date, after the scheduled payments but before finalizing the statements, the note has a single remaining payment of 112.2 in one year. A hypothetical market discount rate is now 20%. Find that present value and compare it with the carrying amount and face. Under the maintained amortized-cost convention, is there an entry solely for this market-rate change? Separately, suppose the lender agrees to accept 97 immediately in full discharge, with no further coupon, fee or other claim. Give the settlement entry, revised cash/assets/liabilities/equity and the revised year-1 indirect CFO when the settlement cash is classified as financing. Explain why 112.2−97 is not the accounting gain.
Complete solutions

  1. At receipt: Dr Cash 60 / Cr Loan liability 60. At 31 March, interest is 60(0.08)(1/4) = 1.2: Dr Interest expense 1.2 / Cr Interest payable 1.2. Relative to the original position, cash and total assets rise 60, liabilities rise 61.2 and equity falls 1.2, so ΔA = 61.2−1.2 = 60. Loan receipt is financing cash; the accrued interest is not yet a cash outflow. Under our paid-interest convention it becomes operating cash when paid. Principal has not been repaid.

    The undrawn 40 contributes neither cash nor sales revenue. It is a separately described potential funding source under its terms. The question stipulates no current fee or other recognized obligation for that facility; this is not a general rule that all commitments require no accounting.

  2. PV = 12/1.1 + 107.8/1.1² = 100. In year 1, expense is 10 and cash coupon 12, so carrying value falls to 98. In year 2, expense is 9.8 and cash paid is 12+95.8 = 107.8, leaving zero. Total expense is 19.8, also total cash 119.8 less initial funding 100.

    Initial premium is 100−95.8 = 4.2. The effective expenses are below coupons by 2 and 2.2, allocating that premium downward. Thus the indirect CFO adjustment for premium amortization has the opposite sign from Ridgeway's discount/fee accretion when coupon cash remains operating. Final principal reduces a previously recognized obligation; recording it as another expense would charge the funding twice.

  3. Net funding and initial liability are 120−7.5 = 112.5. The effective one-year rate is 126/112.5−1 = 0.12. Expense is 13.5. Without the fee, the gross-proceeds yield is 126/120−1 = 5%; the extra cash cost raises the borrower's effective rate even though no cash coupon is called “interest.”

    Record Dr Cash 120 / Cr Note liability 120, then Dr Note liability 7.5 / Cr Cash 7.5. Over the year, Dr Interest expense 13.5 / Cr Note liability 13.5; at maturity Dr Note liability 126 / Cr Cash 126. Total expense 13.5 equals discount 6 plus fee 7.5. Charging 7.5 immediately and also 13.5 through the net-proceeds effective schedule would report 21, overstating the total financing cost by 7.5. Eligibility for this fee treatment was supplied; an unrelated service fee would require its own treatment.

  4. Unpaid-payment PV is 60.5/1.1 + 66.55/1.1² = 55+55 = 110. Initial ROU asset is 110+55 = 165. Record Dr ROU asset 165 / Cr Lease liability 110 / Cr Cash 55. The immediately paid amount is an asset cost, not another future claim.

    Year 1: interest 11; cash 60.5; liability reduction 49.5; closing liability 60.5. Year 2: interest 6.05; cash 66.55; liability reduction 60.5; closing zero. ROU depreciation is 82.5 each year, leaving carrying amounts 82.5 and zero. Total expenses are 93.5 and 88.55, totaling 182.05. Cash is 55+60.5+66.55 = 182.05. Including 55 in both the initial liability and the cash entry would leave a fictitious unpaid obligation or double-count the resource; the timeline prevents that error.

  5. Cash interest is 8+12 = 20 in year 1 and 8+6.6 = 14.6 in year 2. Moving it to financing makes CFO 120 and 100; post-commencement CFF becomes −74 and −184.8. Cash changes from the respective opening positions remain 46 and −84.8. Including commencement, full-calendar 2025 has CFO 120, CFI −80 and CFF 200−74 = 126, increasing cash from zero to 166.

    Under the alternative, indirect CFO adds all financing interest expense back: 18+80+22 = 120 and 3.2+80+16.8 = 100. Do not additionally add note accretion 2 or 2.2, because those amounts are already included in the whole interest addback. Recognition is unchanged, so profit, assets, liability carrying amounts, equity and the year-1 covenant are unchanged. The presentation shift creates no receipt.

  6. With equity injection x, debt stays 168 and equity becomes 88+x. Compliance requires x ≥ 168/1.5−88 = 24. At the minimum, cash is 160, assets 280, debt 168 and equity 112, with 168 = 1.5(112). The injection is financing and does not create revenue.

    With the separately permitted carrying-value retirement y, equity stays 88 and debt becomes 168−y. The minimum is y = 168−132 = 36. Cash falls to 100, assets to 220, debt to 132 and equity stays 88. Because this negotiated settlement is explicitly at carrying value, no gain or loss arises. Both remedies pass the specified repeat test, but the injection leaves 60 more cash than the repayment alternative. Neither remedy exists merely because the arithmetic works: lender consent and actual funding were supplied. A partial retirement also needs a revised coupon, redemption amount and payment calendar before later cash can be forecast; subtracting 36 from a liability alone does not identify those terms.

  7. Second-year operating cash before finance is 160−140 = 20. Scheduled cash payments remain 184.8, so cash ends 166+20−184.8 = 1.2. Profit is 20−20−60−10.2−6.6 = −76.8. Equity ends 118−76.8 = 41.2. Without new funding, assets are cash 1.2 plus owned equipment 40 = 41.2, with old liabilities zero.

    The required buffer needs 10−1.2 = 8.8 of new cash. The expired line and uncommitted proposal supply none. If the stipulated new loan is actually funded, cash becomes 10, assets 50, liability 8.8 and equity 41.2. The new receipt is financing; current-year profit is unchanged because new interest begins after close. Old note and lease liabilities are settled, but new debt of 8.8 remains and its future terms must be disclosed and funded.

  8. The hypothetical market PV is 112.2/1.2 = 93.5, compared with carrying value 102 and face 104.2. A change in that market yield alone creates no entry in the maintained fixed amortized-cost model. The actual full discharge is a separate event: Dr Note liability 102 / Cr Cash 97 / Cr Settlement gain 5.

    Cash becomes 166−97 = 69; owned and ROU carrying amounts remain 60 each, so assets are 189. Lease liability is 66; note liability is zero; equity rises to 123. The balance is 189 = 66+123. Year-1 profit including the settlement gain is 23. Indirect CFO = 23+80+2−5 = 100; the nonoperating gain is removed. Post-commencement financing cash becomes −54−97 = −151, and from commencement cash 120 the net change is 100−151 = −51, ending at 69. Including initial financing 200 and investing −80, full-calendar cash also ends at 100+(200−151)−80 = 69.

    The difference 112.2−97 = 15.2 includes 10.2 of future effective interest that was never accrued at this settlement date. The gain compares cash with the recognized liability: 102−97 = 5. A market quote alone does not prove a lender will accept any of these settlement prices.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain Ridgeway's face 104.2, gross proceeds 102, net funding 100, first-year interest expense 10 and coupon 8 without calling any two interchangeable. Then explain why the lease asset is 60 while the liability is 66 after year 1, and why cash 136 does not cure the stressed covenant breach.

Teach-back guide

Start from contractual cash and eligible fee, derive the PV and carrying rollforward, and separate current expense from payment. The ROU asset follows depreciation while the liability follows interest and settlement. Define the exact covenant D and E; the stressed limit is 132 against debt 168, regardless of positive cash. A complete answer distinguishes recognition, measurement, classification, available funding and legal rights rather than treating one balanced total as proof of all five.

Delayed check, after one week. In Ridgeway's base first year, the coupon of 8 is due but is not paid by the reporting close; everything else occurs as before. Keep the year's accrued interest fixed at 10, with no penalty or extra-day interest. Show the aggregate note obligation including the unpaid coupon, cash, total assets/liabilities, profit, equity, CFO and covenant headroom. The covenant includes that unpaid coupon in D. Does passing its leverage test prove the payment contract was met?

Delayed-check answer

The note is 100+10 = 110 before the missed payment, equivalently scheduled carrying value 102 plus unpaid coupon 8. Cash is 174; assets are 174+60+60 = 294. Liabilities are note 110 plus lease 66 = 176; profit stays 18 and equity 118. Direct CFO is 120−0−12 = 108; indirect CFO is 18+80+10 = 108 because none of the note expense was paid. Financing stays −54, so cash rises 54 from 120. Covenant headroom is 1.5(118)−176 = 1, still nonnegative. Yet a required payment was missed. A leverage pass is not payment compliance, and any acceleration or remedy needs the actual agreement. Paying 8 immediately afterward, absent additional charges, reduces cash to 166 and the aggregate note obligation to 102.

Sources and next steps

The five inspected sources have deliberately different roles: MIT's dated debt instruction supports basic mechanics; archived AASB 9 provisions support the stated cost/effective-interest and extinguishment methods; the IFRS investor explanation and FASB's dated summary bound the lease comparison; and the IASB covenant announcement supports the specific reporting-date distinction. Full current IFRS and US Codification texts have not been compared. Every company, covenant and numerical exercise here is original and synthetic.

Continue through the Volume 7 curriculum to equity claims, group accounts and deeper business analysis. Carry forward a simple discipline: reconcile the recognized balance, then ask who can demand what payment on which date. A beautiful amortization table cannot answer an omitted contractual question.

Sources and further study

  • MIT OpenCourseWare 15.515 Financial Accounting, Fall 2003 — Session 13: Long-term Debt — Dated primary teaching support for face/coupon/market/effective-rate distinctions, discount and premium, issuance/accrual/payment/retirement and book-versus-market value. Original chapter examples are not source exercises.
  • AASB 9 Financial Instruments — December 2022 compiled version — Scoped amortized-cost liability, directly attributable transaction-cost and effective-interest definitions; full extinguishment versus consideration paid. Fees for separate services are distinguished from integral financing fees.
  • IFRS Foundation — Investor Update, September 2020: lessee accounting reminder — Primary explanation of right-of-use asset, present-value lease liability, depreciation and interest as separate amounts. Supports the chapter's bounded lessee model, not a full lease-identification or modification treatment.
  • FASB In Focus — Accounting Standards Update 2016-02, Leases (Topic 842), revised 3 June 2020 — Dated comparison: both US finance and operating leases recognize right-of-use assets/liabilities under the described model, while income/cash presentation differs; operating leases retain a single straight-line expense pattern.
  • IASB — October 2022 announcement: long-term debt with covenants — Dated distinction between reporting-date debt classification and disclosures about covenants to be complied with after that date; announced effective date 1 January 2024.
